{{Short description|Monte Carlo method}}
'''Direct simulation Monte Carlo''' ('''DSMC''') method uses probabilistic [[Monte Carlo method|Monte Carlo]] [[simulation]] to solve the [[Boltzmann equation]] for finite [[Knudsen number]] [[fluid]] flows as part of the field of [[rarefied gas dynamics]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Roohi |first=Ehsan |last2=Akhlaghi |first2=Hassan |last3=Stefanov |first3=Stefan |date=2025 |title=Advances in Direct Simulation Monte Carlo: From Micro-Scale to Rarefied Flow Phenomena |url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-981-96-8200-3 |journal=SpringerLink |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-981-96-8200-3|doi-access=free |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/book/10.1002/9783527685523 |title=Rarefied Gas Dynamics |date=2015-11-25 |publisher=Wiley |isbn=978-3-527-41326-3 |editor-last=Sharipov |editor-first=Felix |doi=10.1002/9783527685523}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Boyd |first=Iain D. |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/nonequilibrium-gas-dynamics-and-molecular-simulation/E317E76AA03C6C2C0A78A67EAB122C30 |title=Nonequilibrium Gas Dynamics and Molecular Simulation |last2=Schwartzentruber |first2=Thomas E. |date=2017 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1-107-07344-9 |series=Cambridge Aerospace Series |location=Cambridge}}</ref>

The DSMC method was proposed by Graeme Bird,<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1063/1.1710976 |title=Approach to Translational Equilibrium in a Rigid Sphere Gas |journal=Physics of Fluids |volume=6 |issue=10 |pages=1518–1519 |year=1963 |last1=Bird |first1=G. A |bibcode=1963PhFl....6.1518B }}</ref><ref>G. A. Bird, ''Molecular Gas Dynamics'', Clarendon Press, Oxford (1976){{page needed|date=March 2018}}</ref><ref>G. A. Bird, ''Molecular Gas Dynamics and the Direct Simulation of Gas Flows'', Clarendon Press, Oxford (1994){{page needed|date=March 2018}}</ref> emeritus professor of aeronautics, [[University of Sydney]]. DSMC is a numerical method for modeling [[Rarefied gas dynamics|rarefied gas flows]], in which the [[mean free path]] of a molecule is of the same order (or greater) than a representative physical [[length scale]] (i.e. the [[Knudsen number]] Kn is greater than 1). In supersonic and hypersonic flows [[rarefaction]] is characterized by Tsien's parameter, which is equivalent to the product of Knudsen number and [[Mach number]] (KnM) or M<math>^2</math>/Re, where Re is the [[Reynolds number]].<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.2514/8.11476 |title=Superaerodynamics, Mechanics of Rarefied Gases |journal=Journal of the Aeronautical Sciences |volume=13 |issue=12 |pages=653–64 |year=1946 |last1=Tsien |first1=Hsue-Shen }}</ref><ref>M. N. Macrossan, 
[http://espace.library.uq.edu.au/view.php?pid=UQ:7959 'Scaling Parameters for Hypersonic Flow: Correlation of Sphere Drag Data']. In: M. S. Ivanov and A. K. Rebrov, ''25th International Symposium on Rarefied Gas Dynamics'', Siberian Division of the Russian Academy of Sciences, p.759 (2007).</ref> In these rarefied flows, the [[Navier-Stokes equations]] can be inaccurate. The DSMC method has been extended to model continuum flows (Kn < 1), and the results can be compared with Navier-Stokes solutions with slip and jump boundary conditions at small Knudsen numbers, i.e., 0.001<Kn<0.1.

The DSMC method models fluid flows using probabilistic simulation [[molecule]]s to solve the [[Boltzmann equation]]. Molecules are moved through a simulation of physical space in a realistic manner that is directly coupled to physical time such that unsteady flow characteristics can be modeled. Intermolecular collisions and molecule-surface collisions are calculated using probabilistic, [[phenomenological model]]s. Common molecular models include the hard sphere model, the variable hard sphere (VHS) model, and the variable soft sphere (VSS) model. Various collision models are presented in.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/j.physrep.2016.08.002 |title= Collision partner selection schemes in DSMC: From micro/nano flows to hypersonic flows |journal=Physics Reports |volume=656 |issue=1 |pages=1–38 |year=2016 |last1=Roohi |first1=E. |last2=Stefanov |first2=S. |bibcode= 2016PhR...656....1R }}</ref>

Currently, the DSMC method has been applied to the solution of flows ranging from the estimation of the [[Space Shuttle]] re-entry aerodynamics to the modeling of [[microelectromechanical systems]] (MEMS).

With the advent of Artificial Intelligence (AI), there are some efforts in combining DSMC and machine learning approaches.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Daultry Ball |first=Nicholas |last2=MacArt |first2=Jonathan F. |last3=Sirignano |first3=Justin |date=2025-12-21 |title=Online Optimisation of Machine Learning Collision Models to Accelerate Direct Molecular Simulation of Rarefied Gas Flows |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0021999125008836 |journal=Journal of Computational Physics |article-number=114601 |doi=10.1016/j.jcp.2025.114601 |issn=0021-9991|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Roohi |first=Ehsan |last2=Shoja-Sani |first2=Ahmad |date=2026-01-01 |title=Data-driven surrogate modeling of DSMC solutions using deep neural networks |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1270963825008569 |journal=Aerospace Science and Technology |volume=168 |article-number=110785 |doi=10.1016/j.ast.2025.110785 |issn=1270-9638|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Tatsios |first=Giorgos |last2=Chinnappan |first2=Arun K. |last3=Kamal |first3=Arshad |last4=Vasileiadis |first4=Nikos |last5=Docherty |first5=Stephanie Y. |last6=White |first6=Craig |last7=Gibelli |first7=Livio |last8=Borg |first8=Matthew K. |last9=Kermode |first9=James R. |last10=Lockerby |first10=Duncan A. |date=2025-01-01 |title=A DSMC-CFD coupling method using surrogate modelling for low-speed rarefied gas flows |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0021999124007484 |journal=Journal of Computational Physics |volume=520 |article-number=113500 |doi=10.1016/j.jcp.2024.113500 |issn=0021-9991}}</ref>

== DSMC Algorithm ==
The direct simulation Monte Carlo algorithm is like [[molecular dynamics]] in that the state of
the system is given by the positions and velocities of the
particles, <math>\{ \mathbf{r}_i, \textbf{v}_i\}</math>, for <math>i = 1, \ldots,
N</math>. 
Unlike molecular dynamics, each particle in a DSMC simulation represents <math>F_N</math> molecules in
the [[physical system]] that have roughly the same position and velocity. 
This allows DSMC to rescale length and time for the modeling of macroscopic systems (e.g., [[atmospheric entry]]). 
Specifically, the system volume is <math>V = (N F_N)/n</math>, where <math>n</math> is the number
density and each collision between simulation particles represents <math>F_N</math> collisions
among molecules in the physical system.
As a rule of thumb there should be 20 or more particles per cubic mean free path
for accurate results.{{citation needed|date=January 2023}}

The evolution of the system is integrated in time steps, <math>\tau</math>, which are
typically on the order of the mean collision time for a particle. 
At each time step all the particles are moved and then a random set of pairs collide.
In the absence of external fields (e.g., gravity) the particles move ballistically as
<math>\mathbf{r}_i(t+\tau) = \mathbf{r}_i(t) + \mathbf{v}_i(t) \tau</math>.
Any particle that reaches a boundary or a surface has its position and velocity reset accordingly
(e.g., [[periodic boundary conditions]]).
After all the particles have moved, they are sorted into cells and some are randomly selected to collide,
based on probabilities and collision rates obtained from the [[kinetic theory of gases]].
After the velocities of all colliding particles have been reset, statistical sampling is performed and then
the process is repeated for the next time step.

=== Collisions ===
On each time step, the particles are sorted into spatial cells and only particles in the same cell
are allowed to collide. Typically, the dimension of a cell is no larger than one-third of the mean free path.
All pairs of particles in a cell are candidate collision partners, regardless of their actual trajectories. For more accurate simulations, the cells are further divided to sub-cells. The subcells can be static or adaptive.

The details of how collisions are calculated in DSMC depend on the molecular interaction model;
here we take the [[hard spheres]] model, which is the simplest.
In the hard spheres model, the collision probability for the pair of particles, <math>i</math> and <math>j</math>, is
proportional to their relative speed,
<math display="block">
P_\mathrm{coll}[i,j] = { {|\mathbf{v}_i - \mathbf{v}_j|} \over
{\sum_{m=1}^{N_\mathrm{c}} \sum_{n=1}^{m-1} |\mathbf{v}_m - \mathbf{v}_n|} }
</math>
where <math>N_\mathrm{c}</math> is the number of particles in the cell and the summations are over particles within the cell.
Because of the double sum in the denominator it can be computationally expensive to use this collision probability directly.
Instead, the following [[rejection sampling]] scheme can be used to select collision pairs:

# A pair of candidate particles, <math>i</math> and <math>j</math>, is chosen at random and their relative speed, <math>v_\mathrm{r} = |\mathbf{v}_i - \mathbf{v}_j|</math>, is computed.
# The pair is accepted as collision partners if <math>v_\mathrm{r} > v_\mathrm{r}^\mathrm{max} \Re</math>, where <math>v_\mathrm{r}^\mathrm{max}</math> is the maximum relative speed in the cell and <math>\Re</math> is a [[continuous uniform distribution|uniform deviate]] in [0, 1).
# If the pair is accepted, the collision is processed; the velocities of the particles are reset but positions are unchanged.
# After the collision is processed or if the pair is rejected, return to step 1.

This procedure is correct even if the value
of <math>v_\mathrm{r}^\mathrm{max}</math> is  overestimated, although it is less efficient
in the sense that more candidates are rejected.

After the collision pair is chosen, their post-collision velocities,
<math>\mathbf{v}_i^*</math> and <math>\mathbf{v}_j^*</math>, are evaluated.
Writing the [[relative velocity]] in terms of [[spherical coordinate system|spherical angles]], <math>\theta</math> and <math>\phi</math>
<math display="block">
\mathbf{v}_\mathrm{r}^* = v_\mathrm{r} [
(\sin\theta \cos\phi) \hat{\mathbf{x}} +
(\sin\theta \sin\phi) \hat{\mathbf{y}} + \cos\theta \,\hat{\mathbf{z}} ]
</math>
these angles are selected by a Monte Carlo process with distributions given by the collision model.
For the hard spheres model, these angles are uniformly distributed over the [[unit sphere]]. 
The azimuthal angle is uniformly distributed between 0 and <math>2\pi</math>, so it is selected as <math>\phi = 2\pi\Re_1</math>
where <math>\Re_1</math> is a [[continuous uniform distribution|uniform deviate]] in [0, 1).
The polar angle is distributed according to the probability density,
<math display="block">
P_\theta(\theta) \, d\theta = {\textstyle \frac{1}{2}} \sin\theta \, d\theta
</math>
Using the change of variable <math>q = -\cos\theta</math>, we have <math>P_q(q) \, dq = ({\textstyle \frac12}) \, dq</math> so 
<math display="block">
-\cos\theta = q ~\mathrm{and}~ \sin\theta = \sqrt{1 - q^2} ~\mathrm{where}~ q = 2\Re_2 -1 
</math>
The post-collision velocities are set as
<math display="block">
\mathbf{v}_i^* = \mathbf{v}_\mathrm{cm}^* + {1\over2}\mathbf{v}_\mathrm{r}^* \qquad
\mathbf{v}_j^* = \mathbf{v}_\mathrm{cm}^* - {1\over2}\mathbf{v}_\mathrm{r}^*
</math>
Note that by conservation of linear momentum and energy, the [[center of mass]] velocity
and the relative speed are unchanged in a collision. That is,
<math display="block">
\mathbf{v}_\mathrm{cm} = {1\over2} (\mathbf{v}_i + \mathbf{v}_j)
= {1\over2} (\mathbf{v}_i^* + \mathbf{v}_j^*) = \mathbf{v}_\mathrm{cm}^*
</math>
and
<math display="block">
v_\mathrm{r} = | \mathbf{v}_i - \mathbf{v}_j |
= | \mathbf{v}_i^* - \mathbf{v}_j^* | = v_\mathrm{r}^*
</math>
This process is repeated for every pair of colliding particles.

From the collision frequency, <math>f_\mathrm{coll}</math>, given by kinetic theory the total
number of hard sphere collisions in a cell during a time <math>\tau</math> is
<math display="block">
M_\mathrm{coll} = {1\over2} (N_\mathrm{c}-1) F_N f_\mathrm{coll} \tau =
{ {N_\mathrm{c}(N_\mathrm{c}-1) F_N \pi d^2 \langle v_\mathrm{r} \rangle \tau}\over
{2 V_\mathrm{c}} }
</math>
where <math>d</math> is the particle diameter and <math>V_\mathrm{c}</math> is the volume of the cell. 
Since collision candidates go through a rejection sampling procedure 
the ratio of total accepted to total candidates for hard sphere particles is
<math display="block">
{ {M_\mathrm{coll}}\over{M_\mathrm{cand}} } =
{ {\langle v_\mathrm{r} \rangle}\over{v_\mathrm{r}^{\max}} }
</math>
The number of collision candidates selected in a cell over a time step <math>\tau</math> is
<math display="block">
M_\mathrm{cand} =
{ {N_\mathrm{c}(N_\mathrm{c}-1) F_N \pi d^2 v_\mathrm{r}^{\max} \tau}\over
{2 V_\mathrm{c}} }
</math>
This approach for determining the number of collisions is known as the ''No-Time-Counter'' (NTC) method.
If <math>v_\mathrm{r}^{\max}</math> is set excessively high then the algorithm processes the same number of collisions (on average)
but the simulation is inefficient because many candidates are rejected.

An alternative, more accurate and time-efficient algorithm is ''Majorant Frequency '' (MF) method, proposed by [[Mikhail Ivanov (scientist)|Mikhail Ivanov]] and Sergey Rogasinsky in 1988.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ivanov |first1=M. S. |last2=Rogasinsky |first2=S. V. |title=Analysis of numerical techniques of the direct simulation Monte Carlo method in the rarefied gas dynamics |journal=Soviet Journal of Numerical Analysis and Mathematical Modelling |volume=3 |pages=453–465 |year=1988 }}</ref>
